title: Forget to Know, Remember to Use: Context-Aware Unlearning for Large Language Models
claim: Unlearning removes target knowledge, but models should still use that knowledge when it is supplied in context, which standard evaluation ignores.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, robot mascots with speech bubbles and thick arrows
description: A wide, three-panel horizontal strip with cartoon robot icons standing for the LLM. Panel (a) Unlearning: a 'Trained LLM' robot receives a speech bubble reading 'Please unlearn Maria Chen' with a group-of-people icon. A thick arrow labeled 'Unlearning' leads to an 'Unlearned LLM' robot with an open folder box and a swirl above its head, suggesting removed data. Panel (b) Direct QA: a user icon with a prompt box asks 'Who is Maria Chen?'. An arrow leads to the Unlearned LLM, which answers 'I don't know'. Panel (c) Contextual QA: a user icon supplies a context bubble (in green) about Maria Chen and a question (in blue). An arrow leads to the Unlearned LLM, whose answer bubble shows '???'. The eye goes first to the robots and bubbles. The final '???' marks the open question of contextual utility.
caption: Overview of our settings. (a) Apply unlearning to remove the forget set; (b) Measure forgetting without additional context. (c) Our new Contextual QA evaluation measures contextual utility by testing whether the model can still use the removed knowledge when it is provided explicitly in the input.
abstract: Large language models may encode sensitive information or outdated knowledge that needs to be removed, to ensure responsible and compliant model responses. Unlearning has emerged as an efficient alternative to full retraining, aiming to remove specific knowledge while preserving overall model utility. Existing evaluations of unlearning methods focus on (1) the extent of forgetting of the target knowledge (forget set) and (2) maintaining performance on the retain set (i.e., utility). However, these evaluations overlook an important usability aspect: users may still want the model to leverage the removed information if it is re-introduced in the prompt. In a systematic evaluation of six state-of-the-art unlearning methods, we find that they consistently impair such contextual utility. To address this, we augment unlearning objectives with a plug-in term that preserves the model's ability to use forgotten knowledge when it is present in context. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach restores contextual utility to near original levels while still maintaining effective forgetting and retain-set utility.
